title: Nationalism and Secularism
shortDescription: Indian nationalism, constitutional secularism, Articles 25–30 and key cases.
genZNote: India's secularism isn't 'religion banished' — it's 'state keeps equal distance'. That nuance is the exam's favourite twist.

sections.heading: Nationalism
bullets: Civic (shared citizenship and constitution) vs ethnic nationalism; Indian nationalism emerged through the anti-colonial movement and stresses unity in diversity.

Gandhi, Nehru and Tagore offered inclusive and critical views of nationalism; the Constitution protects national unity through fraternity and Fundamental Duties (Art. 51A: respect the Constitution, national flag and anthem; uphold sovereignty, unity and integrity).
Challenges: communal and sectarian politics, regional disparities, migration and identity conflicts.

sections.heading: Secularism in India
bullets: The word "secular" was added to the Preamble by the 42nd Amendment (1976), though secularism was already present in the Articles.

Articles 25–28: freedom of conscience and free profession of religion, religious denominations' affairs, no tax for promoting a religion (Art. 27), no compulsory religious instruction in state-funded institutions (Art. 28).
Articles 29–30: cultural and educational rights of minorities; Articles 14–16: equality and non-discrimination.

Indian model: principled distance — the state may intervene for reform (e.g. temple entry, social welfare under Art. 25(2)) and supports all religions equally, unlike strict separation in some Western models.
Judicial position: S. R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994) held secularism to be part of the basic structure.

sections.heading: Communalism
sections.body: Communalism is politics that treats religious identity as the basis of political interests; it is the main threat to constitutional secularism and is addressed through law, education and political practice.

quickRevision.oneLineDefinition: Indian nationalism is inclusive and civic, and constitutional secularism means equal respect to all religions with principled state distance.
keyFacts: Arts. 25–28 freedom of religion; 29–30 minority rights.

highYieldFacts: Art. 27: no tax proceeds for religion.
commonTraps: Do not say India follows strict separation.
